passage: Suraj, you think your grandfather was always this calm about cricket? When I was nine, in our Kanpur lane, my hero was an opener called Vinod Pai. I kept a notebook of his scores, but only the big ones. His ninety-eight against the visitors went in with three underlines. When he got out for two, I told everyone the umpire was blind. When he got out for zero, I said the pitch was wet, just bad luck. My friend Hari once brought the newspaper with the whole season printed: more low scores than high. I tore the page and ran home. That evening my father asked, "Kunal, if another batsman had these scores, what would you call him?" I had no answer, and that question stayed with me longer than any match.

qa.q: What did Kunal say when Vinod Pai got out for zero?
qa.a: He said the pitch was wet, just bad luck.

qa.q: Why did tearing Hari's newspaper page feel right to young Kunal at the time?
qa.a: He felt threatened and embarrassed, because the page attacked a hero he loved, so defending Vinod Pai felt like loyalty, not like ignoring the facts.

qa.q: Which moment became the turning point for Kunal, and why did it work?
qa.a: His father's question about what he would call another batsman with the same scores; it made him judge the numbers without his love for Vinod Pai in the way.

qa.q: How might Hari have felt when Kunal tore the page?
qa.a: Hari probably felt hurt and frustrated, since he had brought the real scores to share and got an angry friend instead.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, he kept only his favourite batsman's big scores and blamed umpires and luck for the low ones.

passage: The power went off in the fifth over, so Samir and his cousin Shankar crowded round Nana's old radio on the balcony, the commentary crackling. "Rajat Dev never fails," Samir announced. "Remember his century in March?" Shankar said nothing about the four ducks since. Then the radio hissed: Rajat Dev, caught behind for six. "That wasn't out! The umpire can't even see in this light," Samir shouted, though he could not see anything either. When the batsman who replaced Dev hit a fifty, Samir shrugged. "Lucky. The ball was old by then." Shankar grinned. "So when your man scores, it's talent, and when anyone else scores, it's luck?" Samir opened his mouth, closed it, and turned the radio up.

qa.q: How was Rajat Dev out, according to the radio?
qa.a: He was caught behind for six.

qa.q: Why did Samir insist the umpire could not see?
qa.a: He felt upset and protective of his hero, so blaming the umpire felt more believable to him than accepting a poor innings.

qa.q: What could Samir try the next time his hero gets out cheaply?
qa.a: He could use the same test for every player, asking whether he would call it bad luck if it happened to someone he didn't support.

qa.q: How does Shankar see Samir's reasoning?
qa.a: Shankar finds it funny and a bit unfair, noticing that Samir calls his hero's runs talent but another player's runs luck.

grounding: During a power cut, a boy explains away his favourite batsman's low score as a bad umpire and calls another player's fifty luck.

passage: On the wall above Hemant's bed in their Pune flat hung a chart: BEST BATSMAN EVER, PRANAV KITTUR. It listed 112, 87, 140 and 95 in thick green marker. "Where's last Sunday?" asked his sister Aparna, pointing. "He made four." "That doesn't count. The ball was swinging because it was cloudy," Hemant said. "And the eleven in Chennai?" "Bad umpire. Everyone knows." Aparna fetched a pencil and wrote 4 and 11 in small grey numbers at the bottom. Hemant rubbed at them until the paper went fuzzy. At dinner he told their father that Kittur had never had a bad season. Aparna raised her eyebrows but let it go, and the grey smudge stayed on the chart.

qa.q: Which scores did Aparna add to the chart?
qa.a: She wrote 4 and 11 in small grey numbers at the bottom.

qa.q: Why did Hemant rub out the pencil numbers?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and protective, because the low scores spoiled the perfect hero he loved, so erasing them felt like keeping the record right.

qa.q: What small step would help Hemant see the whole record?
qa.a: He could keep every score on the chart, good and bad, and look at all of them together before deciding who is best.

qa.q: What is it like for Aparna when Hemant rubs out her numbers?
qa.a: She is probably a little frustrated but chooses not to fight, letting the smudge on the chart speak for itself.

grounding: A boy's wall chart lists only his favourite batsman's big scores, and he blames the weather and the umpire for the low ones.

passage:
Hi Madhuri didi,
You asked about school. Honestly it's fine except for Tejal. I told you she's fake, right? Now I have proof. On Monday she posted "good luck everyone!" before the maths test, which is obviously just for show. On Wednesday she laughed at something Pooja said in the group chat, then an hour later posted a sad quote, so clearly she was mocking her. Pooja agrees with me. And the gossip page the seniors run had two posts about people who act nice for likes, and that's Tejal exactly. I didn't bother reading her long message to me yesterday; it started with "Hey, are you okay?" so it's probably fishing for drama. Mummy says I'm collecting evidence like a detective who already wrote the ending. Whatever. Write back soon.
Usha

qa.q: What did Usha skip reading yesterday?
qa.a: Usha didn't read Tejal's long message, which started with "Hey, are you okay?"

qa.q: Why does Usha feel so sure there is proof against Tejal?
qa.a: Usha feels confident and a bit righteous, because every item noticed fits the view already formed, and the friendly message never gets counted.

qa.q: What could Usha try to check this view fairly?
qa.a: Usha could read Tejal's whole message and list the friendly things Tejal did next to the doubtful ones before deciding.

qa.q: How might Tejal experience Usha's silence?
qa.a: Tejal reached out to ask if Usha was okay, so being ignored could leave her confused and hurt.

grounding: A teenager treats every post by a classmate as proof she is fake, skips her friendly message, and leans on a friend and a gossip page that agree.

passage: Pema, listen, I'm not being dramatic. You know Lavanya doesn't hate people for fun. But Ritvik is fake. His first day, he complimented everyone's handwriting. Who does that? Then in the class group he sent "congrats!!" to Nidhi for the quiz, two exclamation marks, which is too many. And he never replied when I asked about the project, so there. Okay, he did reply later, something about his net being off, I didn't really read it. Also my phone keeps showing me these videos, five signs someone is pretending to be your friend, and he matches like four of them. It's like even the phone agrees with me. What? Why are you looking at me like that?

qa.q: What did Ritvik send Nidhi in the class group?
qa.a: He sent "congrats!!" for the quiz, with two exclamation marks.

qa.q: Why does Lavanya feel certain that Ritvik is fake?
qa.a: Lavanya feels suspicious and sure, because each small act seems to fit, and the videos on the phone make it feel as if the world agrees.

qa.q: What would you advise Lavanya before deciding about Ritvik?
qa.a: Read his late reply properly, notice that the videos only show more of what was already watched, and judge him on a week of plain facts.

qa.q: What might Pema be thinking while listening?
qa.a: Pema may feel uneasy, noticing that Lavanya skipped Ritvik's explanation and treats ordinary friendliness as proof.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend why a classmate is fake, skipping his explanation and trusting a phone feed that keeps showing matching videos.

passage:
Monday. Vikas watched Preeti hand the class monitor a birthday card and muttered to the boy beside him, "Show-off. She wants votes for sports captain." That night he screenshotted her "happy birthday bestie" story and sent it to the boys' group with an eye-roll.
Wednesday. The group chat was full of replies agreeing with him. His phone now kept suggesting clips about fake people, and he watched six. Preeti had messaged him too: "Missed chem? I can send my notes." He left it unopened.
Saturday. Scrolling up to find the chemistry homework, Vikas finally saw her message, sent three days earlier, with the notes attached. He read it twice. Then he scrolled back to the group, where no one had mentioned the notes, because no one knew.

qa.q: What did Preeti offer Vikas on Wednesday?
qa.a: She offered to send her chemistry notes because he had missed chem.

qa.q: How did Vikas probably feel when he finally read Preeti's message on Saturday?
qa.a: He likely felt uneasy and a little ashamed, because the kind message didn't fit the picture of her he had been building all week.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Vikas gathered his proof, and what could fix it?
qa.a: He only looked at things that fit while his group and feed echoed him; reading all her messages and asking someone outside the group would give a fairer view.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Vikas's silence?
qa.a: She may feel ignored and puzzled, since she offered help and got no reply at all.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager collects posts that fit his view of a classmate while his group chat and feed agree, and leaves her kind message unopened.

passage: The placement cell smelled of printer toner. Lakshmi slid her thick folder across Rehana ma'am's desk. "I've done my research. I'm opting out of placements." Inside were eleven printed articles with titles like "Why your first job doesn't matter" and "Build your own path at twenty-one." Clipped to the front was a note from two final-year seniors who had skipped placements and were "doing great." "Did you speak to anyone who skipped and regretted it?" Rehana asked. Lakshmi waved a hand. "Those are people who didn't plan properly." "And the three seniors who came back to us last year asking for off-campus help?" "Different case." Rehana closed the folder gently. "This is a lot of reading. It's all on one side." Lakshmi blinked, then laughed a little too quickly.

qa.q: How many printed articles were in Lakshmi's folder?
qa.a: There were eleven printed articles.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi feel the decision is well researched?
qa.a: She feels confident and proud of how much she has read, without noticing that she only kept articles and seniors who agree with her.

qa.q: What would fairer research look like for Lakshmi?
qa.a: She could talk to the seniors who came back asking for off-campus help and write down the strongest reasons to sit for placements before deciding.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Lakshmi's folder?
qa.a: Rehana sees real effort that only points one way, and is gently concerned that Lakshmi is collecting agreement rather than testing the plan.

grounding: A student brings a folder of articles and seniors' notes that all support skipping placements and brushes off every example that disagrees.

passage:
Subject: Re: placements?
Tanvir bhai,
Thanks for asking, but I've looked into it properly. I'm skipping placements this year and giving the full year to the state services exam. I've read maybe thirty posts from toppers, and nearly all of them say a job divides your focus. Two seniors from my hostel skipped too, and both say it was their best decision. One of them has cleared prelims already. You mentioned that forum thread about people who tried for three years and then struggled to find work; I opened it, but it was mostly people complaining, so I didn't finish it. I also watched a talk saying backup plans make you weaker. So yes, I'm sure. Amma is worried, but she hasn't read what I've read.
Jeevan

qa.q: Which exam does Jeevan plan to give the full year to?
qa.a: The state services exam.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan feel so sure of the plan?
qa.a: Jeevan feels confident and well informed after thirty toppers' posts and two seniors' stories, without noticing that the one thread that disagreed was left unfinished.

qa.q: What would you advise Jeevan to read or ask before deciding?
qa.a: Finish the forum thread, and ask the two hostel seniors what their plan is if the exam doesn't work out, then weigh a job alongside study.

qa.q: Why might Amma react differently from Jeevan?
qa.a: Amma is worried because she sees the risk in the plan, and she hasn't been reading only the success stories.

grounding: A student writes that skipping placements is well researched, citing toppers and seniors who agree while leaving the one disagreeing thread unread.

passage: Manjula, people on campus still ask me, "Santosh, why didn't you sit for placements?" Honestly? By second year I had decided on music, and after that my research was just shopping for agreement. I followed only musicians who had left engineering. I asked the one senior who had made it, not the five who went back to coding. When the head of department sent round the placement numbers, I didn't open the file. I felt very well informed; I had a whole notebook of quotes. Then in final year a friend asked me, "What would make you change your mind?" and I couldn't name a single thing. That scared me more than any exam. I still chose music, by the way. But this time I sat down and read the other side first.

qa.q: Who did Santosh ask for advice in second year?
qa.a: Santosh asked the one senior who had made it, not the five who went back to coding.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel on failing to answer the friend's question?
qa.a: Santosh felt scared and shaken, because having nothing that could change the decision showed the research had only been collecting agreement.

qa.q: Which choice in final year worked better, and why?
qa.a: Reading the other side before choosing music again, because the decision was then tested instead of only supported.

qa.q: What would change if Santosh had opened the placement numbers in second year?
qa.a: Santosh would have faced facts that didn't fit the plan, which might have led to a fairer look at both sides much earlier.

grounding: A young person recalls choosing only musicians and one senior who agreed with skipping placements, and later testing the choice against the other side.

passage: In their Bengaluru flat, Irawati had taped a sheet to the fridge: "Hostel tiffins, 10,000 users by March!" Every evening she read out new comments on her post. "Someone said game-changer!" When a caterer wrote that delivery costs would eat every rupee, she said, "He just doesn't get students." Vaibhav, her flatmate, tried arguing. He listed costs, rivals, licences. She knocked back each point, and each time she dug in harder. On Thursday he tried something else. "Ira, can I say one thing? I've noticed you remember every nice comment word for word, but not a single warning. Is that fair?" She went quiet, stirring her tea. "Okay. That's... fair." Later he saw her open the caterer's comment again and read it to the end.

qa.q: What did the caterer warn about?
qa.a: The caterer wrote that delivery costs would eat every rupee.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav change his approach on Thursday?
qa.a: He felt frustrated that arguing each point only made Irawati dig in harder, and he cared enough to try a gentler way.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Kindly naming the pattern worked, because Irawati could look at her own habit instead of defending the idea point by point.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt when Vaibhav named the pattern?
qa.a: She may have felt caught out but not attacked, which is why she went quiet and later reread the warning.

grounding: A flatmate watches a friend quote every encouraging comment and wave away warnings, and finds that naming the pattern kindly works where arguing did not.

passage:
Across the kitchen table of the flat they shared, Sumit turned his phone round. "Ninety-two likes, Chandrika. Ninety-two. People want campus cycle rentals."
"What did Professor Menon say at the pitch session?"
"That thefts would kill it. But he's old-school."
"And the guard who said cycles vanish from the stand every week?"
"Guards exaggerate."
"And your cousin who asked about repairs?"
"She's just jealous." He tapped the screen. "Look, someone commented 'genius.' Genius!"
Chandrika put down her tea. "Sumit, I'm not going to argue each thing again. Can I just tell you what I keep seeing?"
"...Go on."
"Every like, you quote like evidence. Every warning, you find a reason it doesn't count. That's what worries me, not the cycles."
He laughed, embarrassed. "Ninety-two likes, three warnings, and I only remember one side."
"Yeah."
"Okay. Let's write the warnings down first."

qa.q: How many likes did Sumit's post have?
qa.a: It had ninety-two likes.

qa.q: What worries Chandrika about Sumit's plan?
qa.a: She is worried less about the cycles than about how Sumit treats every like as proof and dismisses every warning.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika's approach work when arguing each point had not?
qa.a: She named the pattern once, kindly, instead of trading facts, so Sumit could see his own habit without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How does Sumit see his idea by the end of the talk?
qa.a: He sees that he has only been remembering one side, feels a bit embarrassed, and agrees to write down the warnings first.

grounding: A flatmate stops arguing point by point and kindly names how her friend quotes every like and dismisses every warning about his startup idea.

passage: Last winter, my roommate Manjula decided to leave final year to build a pet-sitting service. My first move was a mistake. I made a list of seven problems and read them out like a lawyer. She had an answer for each one, and by number four she said, "Mahima, you sound like my father," and stopped looking at me. For the next week she read me every hopeful message she got, and I noticed she never mentioned the vet who'd told her the licensing was tricky. One night I stopped arguing. I said, "Manju, I believe in you. I've just noticed that the good comments stay with you and the warnings slide off. Can we look at the warnings together, once?" She cried a bit, then got her laptop. She's still building it, part-time, and finishing the degree.

qa.q: How many problems did Mahima list at first?
qa.a: Mahima made a list of seven problems.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel, looking back on the lawyer-style list?
qa.a: Mahima feels regretful, calling it a mistake, and was worried enough about Manjula to stop arguing and try a gentler way.

qa.q: What went wrong with the list, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Reading problems like a lawyer made Manjula defend each one; kindly naming the pattern and offering to look at the warnings together opened the door.

qa.q: What was it like for Manjula to hear the pattern named kindly?
qa.a: It seems to have moved her, since she cried a bit and then opened her laptop, feeling supported rather than attacked.

grounding: A roommate recalls how listing problems failed but gently naming a friend's habit of keeping the praise and dropping the warnings helped her rethink.

passage:
"She sent the client file with the old logo again," Rehana said, dropping into the chair beside Faisal. "Told you on day one. Maria's not up to it."
"Again? That's the first time I've heard of it."
"Well, and last week she asked where the templates were."
"Everyone asks that. I asked that."
"And she took forty minutes for a ten-minute task."
Faisal frowned. "The audit summary? The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had."
"Luck. Or someone helped her."
"Rehana, who helped her?"
Rehana opened her mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. I just had a feeling about her from the interview. She seemed nervous."
"So you decided in the interview."
"I didn't decide anything." She stared at the logo on her screen. "Did I?"

qa.q: What did the client say about the audit summary?
qa.a: The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had.

qa.q: Why does Rehana feel her view of Maria is fair?
qa.a: Rehana feels sure and a little irritated, because each small slip seems to confirm the feeling from the interview, so it looks like evidence rather than a first impression.

qa.q: What could Rehana try before judging Maria again?
qa.a: She could write down Maria's good work, like the audit summary, next to the slips, and compare the slips with what other new staff usually do.

qa.q: How might Maria be affected if Rehana's view goes unchecked?
qa.a: Maria could be judged harshly for normal new-starter mistakes, and her strong work might never be credited.

grounding: A young professional reads a new colleague's small slips as proof she is weak and explains away her praised work.

passage: When Deepika joined our design studio in June, she mixed up two clients' colour files in her first week. I decided right then that she was careless. After that I saw it everywhere. A typo in her email? Careless. Five minutes late to stand-up? Careless. When our manager praised her packaging mock-up, I thought, fine, but she probably copied the reference. Then in October our manager said, "Avni, you sit next to her, you do her three-month review," and I had to list examples. My weak column had four small things. Her strong column, when I forced myself to be honest, had eleven, including the redesign that won us the bakery account. I sat there with my coffee going cold, feeling a bit sick. I'd been grading her against a story I wrote in June.

qa.q: How many items were in Deepika's strong column?
qa.a: Eleven, including the redesign that won the bakery account.

qa.q: Why did Avni feel sick while writing the review?
qa.a: Avni felt guilty and uncomfortable on seeing that the careless label from June had been steering every judgment while Deepika's good work was ignored.

qa.q: What habit could help Avni judge new colleagues more fairly?
qa.a: Keep a running list of both strengths and slips from the start, and ask whether the same slip from someone else would even be noticed.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel if she learned about the June label?
qa.a: Deepika might feel hurt and unfairly treated, since one early mix-up coloured how all her later work was seen.

grounding: A young designer looks back on reading every small slip by a new colleague as proof of carelessness while overlooking her strong work.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Pune service desk, 14 March
In today's review Omkar again rated Deepika "below expectations." His examples: one mistyped ticket number in her first week, a late log entry, and a question he called "basic." I checked the system. In the same six weeks she closed the most customer tickets on the team and got two thank-you emails, which Omkar had been copied on. When I showed him the numbers he said, "Maybe, but you can tell she's shaky." He looked genuinely surprised when I asked what she had done since week one that was shaky. He couldn't name anything recent. I've asked him to redo the review using only the ticket log, and I will sit with both of them on Friday.

qa.q: How many thank-you emails did Deepika get in six weeks?
qa.a: She got two thank-you emails, which Omkar had been copied on.

qa.q: Why did Omkar look surprised when asked for recent examples?
qa.a: He felt confident in his view, so it surprised and unsettled him to find it rested on week-one slips, not on anything recent.

qa.q: Why is redoing the review from the ticket log a good step?
qa.a: It makes Omkar work from the whole record instead of a first impression, so Deepika's closed tickets and thank-you emails count.

qa.q: How might Deepika be affected by the Friday meeting?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and fairly seen if her record is finally counted, though it may also hurt to learn how she was rated.

grounding: A supervisor records a young team member rating a new colleague as weak from first-week slips while ignoring her strong ticket record.

passage:
Mentor's note, research team, Hyderabad, Tuesday
Ayesha came to me convinced her new survey design would fix our low response rate. Before asking for sign-off, she did three things I want to record. First, she wrote at the top of her plan: "I'd drop this if the pilot gets fewer replies than the old form." Second, she asked Maria, the analyst who usually picks apart our methods, to find holes in it, and she took notes without defending. Third, she read the paper that argues shorter surveys lose useful detail, and wrote a paragraph on it. Maria found one real problem: a question that led the answer. Ayesha fixed it and thanked her. I approved a small pilot. Next step: we meet in two weeks to read the pilot numbers together.

qa.q: What did Ayesha write at the top of her plan?
qa.a: She wrote that she'd drop it if the pilot got fewer replies than the old form.

qa.q: Why might Ayesha have stayed calm while Maria picked holes in the plan?
qa.a: She seems secure and curious rather than defensive, because she had already decided that criticism would help her find the weak spots.

qa.q: Which of Ayesha's three steps would help most on another project, and why?
qa.a: Writing down in advance what result would change her mind, because it stops her moving the goalposts once the results come in.

qa.q: How does Maria likely see Ayesha after this?
qa.a: Maria probably feels respected and trusted, since Ayesha asked for her toughest view and thanked her for it.

grounding: A mentor records a young researcher setting a test that would change her mind, inviting a sharp critic and reading the case against her before committing.

passage:
Thursday night

passage: At the Shivratri fair in their kasba, Pradeep stopped at a stall hung with shiny cricket stickers. "Fifty rupees for the sheet," said the stall man. Pradeep gasped, then remembered how his uncle bargained. "Forty!" The man shook his head. "Thirty-five, last price." "Done!" Pradeep handed over the coins Nani had given him and skipped back to his sister Aditi. "I saved fifteen rupees!" Aditi looked at the sheet, then at him. "Chintu at school sells these for twenty." Pradeep's grin wobbled. "But he said fifty first. Thirty-five is way less than fifty." "Less than fifty, sure," said Aditi. "Not less than twenty." Pradeep stared at his stickers, suddenly not so sure they were shiny.

qa.q: What price did Pradeep finally pay for the sticker sheet?
qa.a: He paid thirty-five rupees.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep feel he had got a great deal?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited because thirty-five looked small next to the first price of fifty, so it felt like saving fifteen rupees.

qa.q: What could Pradeep try at the next stall?
qa.a: Before hearing the seller's price, he could remember what the same thing costs at school and bargain from that number instead.

qa.q: How does Aditi see Pradeep's bargain?
qa.a: She sees that he still paid more than the school price, and points out that thirty-five is only cheap when compared with fifty.

grounding: At a fair, a boy treats a seller's first price as the fair level, so a still-high price feels like a big saving.

passage: At recess in their school in Porto, Paulo finally spotted it: the shiny goalkeeper sticker he needed to finish his album page. Chen, a year older, held it up. "Ten of your stickers for this one." Ten! Paulo's stomach dropped. He only had twelve spares. "Seven?" he tried. Chen pretended to think. "Eight, and that's me being nice." Paulo counted out eight and hurried away, glowing. "I got him down by two!" he told his friend Tiago. Tiago frowned. "Shinies go for three. Everyone knows that. Beatriz traded one for three yesterday." Paulo looked at his thin stack of four spares. Eight had felt like winning because it wasn't ten. Now it just felt like eight.

qa.q: How many spare stickers did Paulo have left after the trade?

passage: The HR room at the logistics company was freezing. Lakshmi from HR smiled and slid a sheet across. "We're offering three lakh twenty thousand a year for the analyst role." Sonali had spent Sunday reading salary posts; most freshers in this role got between four and five lakh. But now three-twenty was on the table, printed and official, and four suddenly sounded greedy. passage: Farida, you'll laugh, but I learned negotiation by watching Sudhir lose. qa.a: Sudhir may have felt he was bargaining hard while really being pulled toward the supplier's number, which could leave him frustrated with the results.
